title: What fills in the model — judgment?
text: Someone asks whether Claude fills in a financial model using its own judgment like an analyst would. It doesn't. Liam is here to take you through what the skill actually does step by step. The natural guess is that Claude reasons

title: Judgment, or a written list?
text: About your business the way an analyst would deciding what belongs in the model from general financial knowledge. But the skill doesn't work that way. It follows a fixed list of steps written in advance. Ask it to do something those steps don't cover and it won't improvise a fix. It stays exactly inside what's written. What the skill actually does is

title: One number, three statements
text: Read a template that already lays out the three statements and link them together. Watch the anchor. Net income leaves the income statement, lands in retained earnings on the balance sheet, and then shows up again at the top of the cash flow statement. That link is

title: Tied out, not necessarily right
text: Now built. The three statements tie together, and the numbers move where they're supposed to. But a model that ties out isn't the same as a model that's right. The connections can stay consistent even when the assumption feeding them is wrong. And a line that's still blank doesn't mean the run failed. It can mean the template step for that line never got an input to connect. A filled-in model isn't Claude's financial

title: Carry-out
text: Judgment. It's the numbers you gave it linked by a fixed set of steps. The model only connects what the template told it to connect. Your turn. Here's

title: Your turn
text: The prompt. Read it with me. Give Claude a simple set of assumptions, one revenue line, one expense, a starting cash balance, and ask it to run the three-statement model skill and link the three statements. Then change one assumption and watch which lines move and which stay put. That's the fastest way to see the linkage instead of trusting it. Liam in for bear.
